tone_statements.citation: Pacquement, Jean. 2021. "The Tai Meuay of Bolikhamxay Province (Laos) and their language". Presentation slides, 30th Conference of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society (SEALS 30, online), 1 June 2021. 115 slides. Author file linked from the SEALS 2021 programme (Google Drive); talk video: Zenodo, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.5781299.
tone_statements.quote: Summarizing the tonal features of the Phayat variety • 5 tones in A, B, and C columns • 3 tones in DL and DS • Lack of splits in DS column (DS1234) • B-DL quasi-coalescence: B ≈ DL, with B123-4 and DL123-4 B123 [342] ≈ DL123 [343], and B4 [125] ≈ DL4 [124] • B4 [125] and C123 [245] are rising tones, but their contours are different, and there seems to be no merger B4 ≠ C123 is confirmed by the speaker's auditory judgement • B4-C4 coalescence: B4 [125] = C4 [125] [...] Tone systems of all the Tai Meuay varieties dealt with in the literature as well as in this presentation exhibit a tonal coalescence in the DS column.
tone_statements.locator: slide 55 (Phayat tone summary) and slide 96 (DS-column coalescence); per-variety summaries on slides 32 (Keng Bay), 34 (Nava), 45 (Nam Phao), 59 (Thôngkhe), 78 (Hinngôn), 83 (Chomthong), 87 and 91 (Phônsy, Pakkading); slide 38 on the Tai Daeng B4-C123 merger (Gedney 1964)
tone_statements.summary: Southwestern-Tai-type lexical tone on the (mono)syllable: per Tai Meuay variety 5-6 contrastive tones on smooth syllables (one Thôngkhe speaker 9) and 2-3 on checked syllables, with Chao values given (e.g. Phayat B123 [342], B4 [125], C123 [245], C4 [125]); no DS-column split, B-DL (quasi-)coalescence, B4=C4 merger in several varieties, creaky low-falling C4.

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2008. "The Tai dialects of Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong)". In Diller, Edmondson & Luo (eds), The Tai-Kadai Languages, London/New York: Routledge, 298-315. Author's updated French version (2017) 'Les dialectes tai du Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong)', HAL halshs-01617791, 24 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent. Sec. 3 'Généralités phonétiques' (p. 4 of HAL version) states the basic word in Tay Daeng, Tay Yo and Tay Muong is strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T; sec. 4 (pp. 4-6) gives Tay Daeng consonants, vowels (length contrast), and 5- or 6-tone systems for Con Cuông, Mai Châu Thượng and Mai Châu Hạ. a full-text search for stress/accent/tonique/intensité/proéminence/stress: no hits.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tai Daeng language' (downloaded 2026-09-17).
sources.note: Phonology section gives syllable structure and 5 tones on free / 2 on checked syllables, citing Gedney (1989) and Pacquement (2021); no statement on stress.

sources.note: Tone systems only (Gedney-box splits/mergers) for Tai-thaeng, Tai-mot, Tai-moei (= Tai Meuay, tyr), Phu Tai, Nyo and Lao; no mention of stress (a full-text search for stress/accent น้ำหนัก/เน้น/stress: no hits).

sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2009. The Phonology of Proto-Tai. PhD dissertation, Cornell University (eCommons 1813/13855), 438 pp.
sources.note: Comparative reconstruction (Proto-Tai as sesquisyllabic with iambic prosodic words); a full-text search for stress/accent finds no Tai Daeng / Red Tai / Mai Châu data at all, so it says nothing about Tai Daeng stress. Cited by Glottolog only for classification.

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1999. "Les dialectes et les écritures des Tai (Thai) du Nghệ An (Vietnam)". Treizièmes Journées de Linguistique d'Asie Orientale, Paris (EHESS-CNRS), 10-11 June 1999. HAL halshs-00927749, 22 pp. (image-only PDF, scanned with tesseract eng at 150 dpi).
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Covers ethnonyms, informants (Tai Deng of Mai Châu, Tai Thanh of Con Cuông), comparative initials, tones and the scripts; the only 'accent' hits in the scanned text concern Siamese script tone marks.

sources.note: English abstract (read on the DigiVerse API record): classification by tone-box splits; 'The remaining "P" group languages can be subdivided based on tone splits for the A tone. Tai Khun and Tai Yuan form a separate division sharing an A12-34 tone split. Tai yai, Tai Lu, white Tai, Black Tai and Red Tai are grouped together because of their common A123-4 tone split.' Expect a Red Tai (Tai Daeng) Gedney-box tone chart in the data chapters.
